If you could do it over, would you have still chosen to go to college?
Went, never finished. It sounds fun now, but at the time it sucked. High School part two plus alcohol.

Absolutely, with a caveat. The first time I went I was too young to appreciate the true value of higher education. I partied too much and while I technically did not fail out, I basically did. I ended up moving back with my parents, worked fast food, then grounds crew at a golf course where I smoked weed while being outside all day, then went on a long backpacking trip overseas. Basically, I enjoyed being young and having freedom.

Eventually I went back to school, triple majored/ double degree for my undergrad, finishing near the top of my class and now I am trying to finish up a phd. I say this not to brag, but to illustrate the point that if would do it over again, I wouldn't have wasted the time and money trying to force it as early as I did. I didn't know what I wanted to do with my life the first go at university. The second I had a goal and was driven to succeed. University is too expensive to flounder around, at least in the US.

I may end up getting in trouble with the administration one day or get an earful from a pissed off parent, but I share this story with every floundering, under-preforming undergrad I have been a TA and course instructor for. I suggest that they should seriously consider taking a gap year and sort out things in their life before they waste any more time or money.

That's awesome. I took a gap semester+summer before junior year and was so excited to go back to school that I bought my textbooks and started working through them before summer ended. I could have afforded to take a break earlier though. It was still a bit of a shock graduating, hitting the real world, and not knowing quite what I wanted in life and work.

I went but left. I went my 20s without college and it was a struggle. Lots of ups and downs. I stopped caring about college once I befriended loads of college grads in my late 20s that earned less than me and struggled just as much as I had but have loads of debt looming over them as well. One guy I knew was 40k in debt and became homeless and he went to a prominent uni and earned a bachelor's degree. I have enough experience behind me now that it's not difficult for me to find work. HR cares more about experience than college. College is more an opportunity to learn socialising and networking really. I moved out of the US and can got college free where I live now. I've considered trying to get a degree in IT but I doubt it is worth the effort. I'd only earn a couple thousand a year more than I do now.

I went right after high school for two years and burned myself out. I later went back and finished up on a different degree path. I wished I would have stuck out the first time and got that degree.

I also later returned to school to get a law degree. I do not regret getting the law degree, but I do regret the cost involved (not just monetary cost).

Yes. Even though in the 28 year career that followed I used exactly 1 thing that I learned while getting an under graduate degree in CompSci. One of our profs spoke at the CS grad and made the point that the value of our time here wasn't what we learned, but rather that we learned how to learn. It really struck a chord at the time and, as you can see, has stuck with me.

Doing hiring in IT over the years I really noticed a difference between grads from Unis and grads from technical schools. The tech school grads were almost all just interested in getting a job and were not eager to learn new things. I'm not saying there weren't exceptions but the trend was clear to me. I'm not saying tech school grads were bad hires, but I am saying that generally speaking they were better suited for certain jobs. Just like Uni grads were better suited for certain jobs. Though TBH the best hires were those who loved computers for their own sake, these guys (sorry, never had a girl applicant that I would include in this group) were all self taught and other than specific certs whether they'd also attended post 2ndary school was irrelevant.

Anyhow even back then a good number of the students were graduating with arts or science degrees that were pretty useless in terms of finding a job in that field. But then 4 years of partying didn't result in a $100K debt so it wasn't like it is today.
I havnt graduated yet but i cant imagine not going to college. Make tons of friends, i have learned a ton of stuff, and hopefully ill land a solid 80k job once ive finished up.
